In a little town by the sea, there lived an Owl. His feathers were pale brown and his eyes were very round. Every evening he sat on the windowsill with an old guitar and sang one slow song to the water. Next door lived a Pussycat whose fur was the colour of cream left in the sun. She liked to sit at the other end of the sill and listen, and her tail kept time, softly, softly.
One day she said, let us go and see what is on the other side of the sea. In the morning the Owl brought round a pea-green boat. They took a jar of honey, a few bright coins, and a small note with good night on it, in case they came home too late to say it. The Pussycat folded the note into a tiny paper boat and put it in her pocket.
The sun was going down when they pushed off. The water turned the colour of honey, and the wind was so light it only filled the sail a little.  The Pussycat trailed one paw in the water, watching the silver light open in rings. Time at sea was slow enough to count every single star.
When the sky was quite dark they came to a small bay with trees along the shore. A Pig was standing there, taking a little ring off his nose and putting it into a basket. He had saved a long time for it, he said, but he could not wear it all by himself. The Pussycat looked at the Owl, and the tips of his ears went pink. So they bought the ring for one penny and asked a passing Turkey to do the thing properly in the moonlight.
It was not a grand affair. The sand was white with moon, and the waves kept smoothing away their footprints. The Pussycat put on the ring, the Owl held the guitar steady, and played a tune slower than the one he had sung by day. They danced on the wet sand. The moon moved a little to one side, as if to make room.
Late on, the honey was almost gone, but nobody minded. The Owl spread his coat in the bottom of the boat. The Pussycat set the little paper boat on the water and watched it bob away. They lay down side by side and listened to the water tap the hull, slower than any song. Shall we go on tomorrow, asked the Owl. Let us sleep first, she said. The sea is not going anywhere.
If you hear a very soft lapping outside your window tonight, it is probably that pea-green boat passing by. There is a jar with a little honey left, an old guitar, and two small travellers already asleep. You do not need to get up and look. Just pull the blanket close and let your breathing follow the water, one wave, then one wave. Good night, little cat, and good night to you.

At the edge of the village there was a large garden. The grass was as green as something just washed, and every spring twelve peach trees flowered all at once until the wall turned pink. The garden belonged to a Giant who had gone visiting, and he stayed away seven years. All that time the children came in after school and played on the grass, and the birds sang from the boughs.
Then one day the Giant came home. He saw the children everywhere and frowned, and his voice was loud enough to shake the snow off the roof. This is my garden, he said. He built a high wall and hung up a board that said keep out. So the children had to stay outside. They walked round the wall and put their eyes to the cracks, saying how happy they had been in there.
Spring came as usual. Small flowers opened all over the village. Only the Giant's garden stayed winter. Snow lay on the grass, frost hung on the branches, and the wind would not come in. The Giant sat wrapped in a blanket, waiting day after day for one flower. He could not understand it. The sun reached this place too, did it not.
Then one morning a small bird note woke him, a sound he had not heard for a long time. He ran to the window and saw children squeezing through a gap in the wall, climbing into the peach trees. The moment a branch was touched it hurried into flower, like someone finally letting go of a long breath. The snow drew back from the grass and the green showed through.
Only the farthest corner stayed white. A very small boy stood there, too short to reach a branch, stretching up on tiptoe again and again, his eyes full of hurry. The Giant walked out, and the garden went quiet. All the children ran, except that one, because when he looked up there was no fear in his face at all, only a small hope of being lifted.
The Giant lifted him gently onto the highest branch. The tree broke into blossom at once, and the birds came back and settled on the Giant's shoulder. He understood then: spring had not forgotten this place; he had shut spring outside. He turned and pushed the wall down, brick by brick, trod the board into the earth, and called over the gap, come back, the garden is yours. The children had never run so fast.
After that the garden never saw winter again. The Giant often sat on the grass while children climbed up and down his legs, and petals caught in his hair. When he was old he watched them from a chair and said the best spring was the one with someone in it. If there is a tree outside your window tonight, do not worry that it has not flowered yet. Sleep first. By daylight spring will find the door by itself. Good night, Giant, and good night to you.

On Christmas morning a small velveteen rabbit was tucked into a stocking full of presents. He had brown and white fur, pink satin inside his ears, and whiskers made of thread that felt a little scratchy. He was shy at first, because the other toys were so grand: a clockwork train, a painted horse, and a bear that spoke when pressed.
They took little notice of him and said he was only cloth. Only the old Skin Horse in the corner told him the important thing, slowly. Being real is not about what you are made of, he said. It is about whether a child truly loves you. Love someone long enough and even loose stitches and rubbed-away fur become real. How long does it take, asked the rabbit. There is no telling, said the horse. Sometimes it takes a long time. Sometimes it happens all at once.
That night the Boy found him by the pillow, gathered him up, and never chose another toy again. In the daytime he rode in the little cart. At night he lay under an arm, a cheek against the soft ear, listening to things said in a voice meant for two. Once he was left out in the garden all night in the rain. The next morning the Boy held him without a word, tears in his eyes, and kept him wrapped close for a long time.
The days went on. The fur wore thin, the pink satin faded to grey, one ear folded over, and a few whiskers went missing. The rabbit did not mind. He could read the Boy's breathing now: slower meant nearly asleep, and the slowest, most even stretch was the moment to let go. Perhaps this is what the horse meant, he thought.
Then the Boy was ill and stayed in bed a long while. The rabbit was kept by the pillow. At night the lamp was turned low, and a hand came to tuck the blanket in. The Boy hardly spoke. He only laid a hand on the rabbit and rubbed the bald place with one finger, over and over. The rabbit wished he could be warmer for him. There was nothing he could do except stay exactly where he was, and not move away.
One night the fever broke and the Boy slept with his hand still there. Moonlight lay on the folded ear. The rabbit suddenly thought that the loose threads and the missing fur were not ugly at all. They had been made by being held, one day at a time. He stopped wondering whether he was real, because he was already needed, properly and quietly, in someone's arms. That was enough.
If you are holding something old and a little bald tonight, do not mind how it looks. It remembers every night you have fallen asleep. Settle it beside you, put your face against it, and let tonight become one more it remembers. The lamp can go out now. Good night, little rabbit, and good night to you.

In one corner of the farmyard lived a little red hen. Her feathers were the warm colour of brick. She shared the yard with a cat, a duck and a pig. The cat lay on the wall in the sun. The duck stirred the pond into circles. The pig rolled in the mud and sighed.
One morning she found a few grains of wheat by the straw stack, plump and golden. If I plant these, she thought, there will be bread in the autumn. So she went and asked, who will help me plant this wheat. The cat narrowed his eyes to a line and said not I. The duck put his head under water and mumbled not I. The pig rolled over and said not I either. The little red hen nodded. Then I will do it myself, she said.
She scratched a short row of soft earth beside the fence, pressed each grain in one by one, and smoothed the soil over them. For many days after that she went out early to look. When it rained she worried, and when the sun shone she worried about the dryness. When the shoots came up in a thin green line, she went twice round the yard for joy.
The wheat grew tall and bent its heavy heads. It was time to cut. She asked once more, who will help me harvest. Not I, said the cat. Not I, said the duck. Not I, grunted the pig. So she cut and dried the wheat alone and rubbed the grains into a small cloth sack.
The grain had to go to the mill. The road was not long, but the sack was heavy. She stood in the middle of the yard and asked one last time, and got the same three answers. She only shifted the sack higher and set off slowly. When the mill wheel turned, white flour fell into the bowl like fine snow.
By evening the kitchen was warm. She mixed the flour with water and a pinch of salt, and set the dough by the stove to rise slowly. The cat, the duck and the pig had come to the doorway and watched in silence. When the bread came out the whole room smelled of it, the crust golden and steam rising as it broke. Only then did they each move half a step forward and ask, quietly, may we share it.
The little red hen thought for a moment, and she did not say no. She broke the loaf into several pieces, handed one to each of them, and kept the smallest corner for herself. I did the planting and the cutting and the milling and the baking, she said, but bread is not good eaten alone. Outside, the light was going, and the yard grew quiet except for the sound of chewing. If you smell warm bread tonight, do not get up. It is only someone putting the day away for you. Close your eyes. Good night, little red hen, and good night to you.

Once there were three very small names: Wynken, Blynken and Nod. They lived in a wooden shoe with a toe that curled up like a new moon. Every night, when the last lamp in the house had gone out, they pushed the shoe into the silver river above the roof, untied the rope, and drifted slowly away.
That river was not made of water. It was made of starlight. Clouds floated on it, as soft as cotton freshly teased out, and each of the three carried a little net on a fine thread. They were not fishing. They were catching dreams. A caught dream was quite clear, and when you tipped it gently there was a small picture inside: sometimes a balloon, sometimes a biscuit only half eaten, sometimes a kind word that had gone missing during the day.
Wynken cast his net the furthest. Blynken watched to see whether any stars had fallen in. Nod, who was the smallest, said a tiny oh whenever they brought up an especially lovely one. One night they caught a very bright star that shivered as though it had just woken. Do not be afraid, said Nod, we are not keeping you. They opened the net, and the star rose slowly back to its own place and shone a little brighter than before.
Higher up the river grew quieter. There were no houses on either bank and no lamps, only a thin mist washed over by the moon. The wooden shoe went by itself. Nobody rowed and nobody steered. The three sat in a row with their feet hanging out, listening to the sole brush the starlight, hush, hush, softer than a page being turned.
Once the wind rose and the clouds drew together and covered the river for a while. Nod was a little frightened and asked whether they might lose their way. Wynken pointed to the one star that never moved, high above. That is the lamp at our door, he said. As long as it stays, we can get home. Blynken folded the nets up and spread them over all three like a blanket. When the clouds parted, they were already asleep, with a few undisturbed dreams lying in the folds.
Just before daylight the wooden shoe drifted back to the windowsill by itself. Their mother always said there was fine silver dust on the pillow that no brushing quite removed. Wynken, Blynken and Nod never explained. They only folded the nets, stood the shoe back against the wall, and yawned all day. For those three names are really two eyes, two eyes, and one small head that keeps nodding.
Tonight, if you close your eyes and feel yourself sinking gently, that is the wooden shoe setting out again. Do not open them, do not count the stars, and do not worry about the way back. The nets will keep the best small piece of today for you, and the lamp will wait exactly where it was. Hush, hush. Good night, Wynken. Good night, Blynken. Good night, Nod. And good night to you.

Once upon a time, a little girl was loved by everyone, but most of all by her grandmother, who made her a red velvet cape with a hood. Because she wore it so often, people called her Little Red Riding Hood.
One day her mother said, "Take this basket of cakes and wine to grandmother, who is not well. Stay on the path and do not wander."
Red Riding Hood set off through the woods. A Wolf wanted to eat her, but dared not in the open. He asked where she was going, and she told him. The Wolf ran ahead to grandmother's cottage, knocked, and when the old woman opened the door, he swallowed her up and put on her clothes in bed.
When Red Riding Hood arrived, she noticed grandmother looked strange.
"Grandmother, what big eyes you have!"
"All the better to see you, my dear."
"What big teeth you have!"
"All the better to eat you!" And the Wolf sprang at her.
But a passing woodsman heard the noise and rushed in. He saved Red Riding Hood and her grandmother, and they all sat down to the cakes together.
So, little one, remember to stay on your own safe path, and gentle helpers are never far away. Close your eyes now, and dream of warm cakes and safe woods.

There was once a kind girl whose father married a woman with two daughters of her own. After he died, the stepmother made the girl do all the work, and they called her Cinderella.
One day the Prince invited every maiden to a grand ball, hoping to choose a bride. Cinderella's stepmother said she could not go. But as she sat crying, her fairy godmother appeared and, with a wave, turned a pumpkin into a coach, mice into horses, and a ragged dress into a gown of silver with glass slippers.
"But the magic ends at midnight," said the godmother.
At the ball, the Prince danced only with Cinderella. As the clock began to strike twelve, she ran, leaving one glass slipper behind.
The Prince searched the kingdom for the maiden whose foot fit the slipper. When he came to Cinderella's house, her stepsisters tried and failed. Cinderella slipped her foot in, and it fit perfectly.
The Prince married her, and they lived with kindness in their hearts. So, little one, goodness is its own quiet magic. Close your eyes, and let sweet dreams carry you to the ball.

Once there was a princess named Snow White, with skin as white as snow and a kind heart. Her stepmother, the Queen, was jealous and asked her mirror every day who was fairest. When the mirror said Snow White, the Queen sent a huntsman to take her into the forest.
The huntsman could not harm her and told her to run. Snow White found a tiny cottage belonging to seven dwarfs, who let her stay if she kept house.
The Queen learned she was alive and came disguised as an old woman, offering a poisoned apple. Snow White bit it and fell into a deep sleep. The dwarfs could not wake her and laid her in a glass coffin.
One day a Prince rode by, saw her, and kissed her forehead. The apple slipped from her lips, and she awoke. The Prince took her to his castle, and the jealous Queen's vanity was ended.
So, little one, a kind heart sleeps safely and wakes to love. Close your eyes now, and let the dwarfs watch over your dreams.

A Princess once dropped her golden ball into a deep well. She cried, and a Frog offered to fetch it if she would be his friend and let him eat from her plate and sleep on her pillow. She promised, and the Frog brought the ball back.
At first the Princess did not want to keep her word, but her father said a promise must be kept. So the Frog came to the palace. That night, when he asked to sleep on her pillow, she lifted him gently, and suddenly he became a Prince, who had been cursed by a wicked fairy.
They became friends, and soon the Prince's kingdom and the Princess's were joined in happiness.
So, little one, keeping a promise can wake the magic hidden in the world. Close your eyes, and dream of golden balls and gentle frogs.

In a time of hunger, a woodcutter's wife led his two children, Hansel and Gretel, into the forest and left them there. But Hansel had dropped white pebbles on the way, and they followed them home by moonlight.
The next time, she took them deeper, and Hansel could only drop crumbs, which the birds ate. Lost, the children found a cottage made of bread, cakes, and sugar. An old woman invited them in, but she was a witch who meant to eat them.
Gretel was clever. When the witch told her to look in the oven, Gretel pushed the witch in and shut the door. The children found treasure, and a friendly duck carried them across the river home, where their father was overjoyed.
So, little one, when you are lost, be brave and clever, and you will find your way home. Close your eyes now, and let the pebbles of the moonlight guide your dreams.

On a cold New Year's Eve, a little girl walked barefoot through the snow, holding matches to sell. No one bought any, and she was too afraid to go home.
She sat in a corner and lit one match. In its warm glow she saw a great iron stove, then a table of roast goose, then a beautiful Christmas tree. With the last match, she saw her grandmother, who had loved her, smiling and reaching out.
"Take me with you," whispered the girl. And her grandmother took her up, and they flew together into the light and warmth, where there was no cold and no hunger.
So, little one, even on the coldest night, love keeps you warm. Close your eyes now, and let grandmother's light carry you to a soft, safe sleep.

There was an Emperor who loved fine clothes. Two swindlers came and said they could weave a cloth so wonderful that only the wise could see it. In truth, they wove nothing at all.
The Emperor sent them gold, and they pretended to work. When he sent ministers to look, each was afraid to seem foolish, so each said the cloth was beautiful.
At last the Emperor paraded through the city in his new clothes, which were no clothes at all. The people, not wanting to seem unwise, cried how splendid he looked.
Then a small child called out, "But the Emperor has nothing on!"
And everyone whispered the truth.
So, little one, it is always brave and kind to tell the simple truth. Close your eyes now, and dream of honesty as bright as the sun.
